Arianna had been avoiding that question all week. At home she had assumed the whole portfolio would go, all ten, the full sustained body of work, and the scoring would simply absorb it. Then Brian had said something in the dining hall that had knocked the arrangement sideways in her head, and she had gone to the cabin that night and read the requirements on her phone until the screen dimmed. The Selected Works section of the AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio asked for only five artworks, and it counted for 40 percent of the score. Five out of her ten. The other section carried the rest, but the five she chose would be nearly half of everything, hanging there alone under the lights without the statement beside them to explain what she had been trying to do.

"Five," she said now. "Brian says five."

Brian arrived before Claire could answer, carrying his own portfolio under one arm, hair still wet from the lake. He was already arguing, the way he argued, mercurial one minute and precise the next. "You send the technical ones," he said. "The dishpan hands, the lake, the puddle. The ones where you can draw. The storm drain is conceptual and conceptual reads as risky when there's no statement taped next to it."

"That's exactly backwards," Claire said. "The five are the only ones that speak for themselves. You send the strange ones so they look like choices, not accidents."

Arianna looked from one to the other. She wanted to beseech them to just decide for her, to tell her which five were hers, but she made herself close her mouth and pick up the storm drain painting instead. It was the newest, the least sure: tar-black water curling through a grate, painted with a palette knife because the brush had felt too polite. She had made it the week the rain wouldn't stop and the lower path had washed out and the whole camp had smelled of wet cedar.

She carried it to the window and held it against the light. Her grandmother's hands, done in the third week, were the best drawing she had ever produced; she knew that the way she knew her own handwriting. But the storm drain was the reason the other nine existed, the moment the theme had stopped being a pretty phrase and become an argument: that water keeps what passes through it, that a place can hold a history in something that drains away. Brian wanted the evidence of skill. Claire wanted the evidence of intention. Somewhere between them was a position she could actually defend, though she could not yet say what it was.

Mr. Warsame came through the barn on his rounds, checking the hanging wires for the evening show, and paused at her floor of paintings. He did not offer an opinion. He only said, "Statement on the table by noon tomorrow, and label everything," and moved on to the next easel, which was exactly the kind of adult he was.

That night, after lights-out, Arianna sat on the cabin porch with the storm drain painting across her knees and a flashlight balanced on the railing. She wrote in the margin of her sketchbook: skill is what I can prove, intention is what I mean, and the portfolio is the dialectic between them, unresolved on purpose. Then she crossed out the last three words because they were a lie. It was unresolved because she was eighteen and had made ten things about water in a summer, and she did not yet know which of them were art and which were practice, and no one was going to tell her.

By midnight she had circled five in pencil, erased two, and circled a different two. In the morning she wrote the statement, four sentences, then cut it to three. At noon she carried the paintings to the barn, and Claire held the hanging wire while Arianna lifted the storm drain into its clip, first in the row, where the sequence would begin.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: The Gulf Stream leaves the US coast near Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, and turns northeast across the Atlantic.
story:
Eve spread the current map across the picnic table and pinned its corners with two mugs and a dish of peaches that were going soft. The map had come from Mr. Nasser's classroom, borrowed without asking, and it showed the Atlantic in arrows: cold ones drawn blue and thin, warm ones red and fat as garden hoses. Karis sat across from her with her feet on the bench, eating a peach like it owed her money.

"Quiz me," Eve said.

"Okay. Why is Ireland not frozen solid?"

"That's what I'm trying to figure out."

"You're the one who told Simona you had this handled." Karis worked the pit loose with her teeth. "She's inside right now telling your mom you have it handled."

The screen door slapped and Simona came out with a bowl of ice, which she set down nowhere near anybody. "I told your mom you were studying oceanography like a scholar. She seemed very relieved. She used the word erudition."

"She used it last week about the dishwasher manual," Eve said.

"Then it means something different at your house than it does at mine."

Eve bent over the map. The red arrow ran up the coast, hugging the shoreline like something following a wall, and then, off a notch of land labeled North Carolina, it swung away. It didn't drift out gradually. It turned. She put her finger on the bend.

"Why here," she said. "Why not keep going north along the coast?"

"Maybe the coast ends," Karis said.

"The coast doesn't end. Canada is up there. It goes on for ages."

"Then maybe the arrow's shy."

Simona leaned in over her shoulder, breathing peach and mint. "It's like a hose," she said. "You know when you're watering and you swing the nozzle? The water doesn't go where the nozzle goes, it goes off sideways."

"That's not how a current works."

"You asked why. I offered a hose."

Eve had been telling herself for two weeks that she could compartmentalize the whole thing. The failed quiz in one drawer, the retake tomorrow in another, and in a third drawer, the one she kept shut, the fact that Mr. Nasser had said, in front of everyone, "Eve will explain the Gulf Stream for us Thursday, since she finds it so intuitive." She had found nothing intuitive in her life. She had found the word humiliating and had smiled at it like it was a compliment, which was its own kind of failure.

The afternoon light came slantwise through the fence and lit the map so the red arrow looked almost orange where it curved. She traced it again. It leaves the coast, she thought. Here, at this notch. Cape Hatteras. She said it aloud. "Cape Hatteras."

"Bless you," said Karis.

"It's where the current leaves the US coast. North Carolina. And then it turns northeast across the Atlantic." She followed the arrow with her finger, across the whole cold gray of the printed ocean, toward the small clustered shapes of Ireland and Britain and the edge of Norway. The red thinned as it went, and somewhere in that thinning, warmth. Enough warmth, apparently, that palm trees could survive in Ireland and London rain never quite froze. Heat carried like a letter across an ocean and delivered to the wrong latitude.

"So the water's warm," Simona said, "and warm water heats the air, and the air goes to Ireland."

"Something like that."

"You don't sound sure."

"I'm sure about the arrow. The rest I'm still holding loosely."

Next door, the sound of Mr. Nasser's lawnmower choked and died. Then his head appeared over the fence, sweat-shined, cheerful in a way Eve distrusted. "Is that my map?"

"I was going to return it Monday."

"Monday is the retake. You know that, correct?" He said it gently, which was worse. Karis suddenly found the ice bowl fascinating. Simona examined the sky.

"I know," Eve said. She had not told them. She had let them believe Thursday was a presentation she'd volunteered for, an honor, and now the word retake sat on the picnic table among the peach pits where everyone could see it.

"I'll make a deal," Mr. Nasser said. "You explain the map to me right now, over this fence, and if you get it wrong, you return the map tonight and study from the textbook like a normal person. If you get it right, you keep it until Thursday."

Eve stood up. The map was a poor thing to stake anything on, a wrinkled page with a borrowed history, but it had become the whole of it anyway. She put her finger at the notch. "The Gulf Stream leaves the US coast near Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, and turns northeast across the Atlantic. It carries warm water toward northern Europe. That's why Ireland isn't frozen."

Mr. Nasser rubbed his jaw with the back of his glove. Behind her, Karis had stopped chewing.

"And why does it turn?" he asked.

"I don't know yet."

"Then say that tomorrow too. The part you know, say it plainly. The part you don't, say you don't. Don't pad it. Half of erudition is knowing where your knowledge is impermeable."

"That's not half of anything," Eve said. "That's just honesty with a bigger vocabulary."

Mr. Nasser laughed, a real one, and dropped below the fence. The mower coughed back to life. Simona scooped ice into the mugs, and Karis, without being asked, put a fresh peach beside Eve's hand.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: Higher interest rates pay savers more, so households tend to shift some money from spending into savings, which lowers demand for goods and helps slow price rises.
story:
The bank letter had come on Tuesday, folded into the same envelope as his statement, and Carson had read it three times before he understood it was good news: the savings rate on his account had gone up. He was sixteen, with a summer job bagging groceries and a lemonade stand on the corner of Alder Street, and he had been saving since June for a phone that cost more than he wanted to admit out loud. The new rate changed the arithmetic. Money left alone in the account would now grow faster than it had a month ago, quietly, without him doing anything at all.

The problem was that the phone went on sale until Sunday, and today was Saturday. If he bought it, the price dropped enough to feel like a decision. If he waited, the savings rate would keep paying him to hold on. He could not do both, and the stand in front of him, with its hand-lettered sign and its pitcher sweating in the heat, was where he intended to think it through, because thinking at home meant his mother offering opinions.

Jenny arrived first, on her bike, one hand holding a folded newspaper she'd been carrying around all week like evidence. "Two cups," she said, dropping quarters on the table. "Did you see they raised rates again?"

"Sort of," Carson said. "My bank raised what it pays on savings. I got a letter."

Jenny slapped the paper down beside the cash box. "That's the same thing. My dad keeps saying it's supposed to fix inflation, and I keep asking how, and he keeps saying ask Ms. Pereira." She pulled a face. "I have her Monday. I wanted to actually sound like I understood it before then."

River came around the corner with his own cup already, stolen from somewhere, and settled onto the curb. "I understood it for about an hour last spring," he said. "Then it evaporated."

Carson poured, and because pouring gave his hands something to do, his mind loosened. "Okay, so here's the part I actually get," he said. "When rates go up, savings accounts pay more. So people like me look at the account and think, I'd rather have that money sitting there earning than sitting in my pocket waiting to be spent."

"Okay," Jenny said slowly.

"So imagine everyone doing a smaller version of that. Households shift some money from spending into savings, because saving pays better now. And then," and here he paused, because he was assembling it in real time, watching it fit, "if people are spending less on stuff, then there's less demand for the stuff. Fewer people fighting over the same phone, the same groceries, the same lemonade. And when demand drops, prices stop climbing so fast. That's the inflation slowing."

River was squinting at him. "Where did you get that?"

"Nowhere. I got the first piece from the letter, and the rest just now, out loud, because Jenny asked." He felt slightly untrustworthy of his own conclusion, the way he did when an answer came too easily on a test. "I might be imputing too much to one envelope from the bank. Maybe my decision about a phone isn't the whole economy."

"It's a piece of it, though," Jenny said. "Multiply you by everybody."

The stand had gone quiet, the three of them looking at the pitcher, at the coins, at the heat shimmer over the asphalt. A woman bought a cup for her kid and paid with a dollar and exact change, and Carson made change without thinking, and thought about how many transactions like this one made up whatever a polity was, all these small yeses and noes at cash registers adding up to a direction nobody had voted on directly.

"So what are you going to do?" River asked. "Phone or savings?"

"That's the thing. The sale ends tomorrow night, and the new rate doesn't. It's like the two of them are arguing." He turned the letter over in his head. "The bank is basically paying me to be patient, and the store is paying me not to be."

"You could be circumspect," Jenny offered. "That's my word of the week. It means careful, sort of looking at everything before you decide."

"I know what it means," Carson said, but not unkindly. "I'm trying. It's just, I can't actually tell which one wins. If I save, that's the rate working on me exactly the way it's supposed to. If I spend, I'm the demand they're trying to cool down. Either way I'm inside the machine, and I can't see the machine."

River drained his cup. "So pick the one you can live with when you're wrong."

Carson looked down the street toward the bank, four blocks of it visible from the stand, its sign plain and white in the sun. He picked up Jenny's newspaper, folded it back along its creases, and handed it to her. "Monday, when she asks, tell it the way I told it just now. And tell her you still don't know why it works, only that it does."

Jenny took the paper and said, "What about your phone?"

Carson opened the cash box, counted what the afternoon had brought, and poured himself the last of the pitcher.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: Many people prefer $50 now over $100 in a year, yet prefer $100 in six years over $50 in five, a preference reversal called present bias.
story:
The screen door banged twice before Jake got it to close, and his grandfather's ledger lay open on the kitchen table where he had left it, a clothbound book with entries in fountain pen going back further than his parents had been alive. He had come out to the house for the weekend to help clear it, his mother said, though everyone knew clearing it meant deciding what happened to it now that his grandfather was in the home and not coming back.

Ulysse had come along for the drive, and Kayleb arrived an hour later on his bike with a clipboard, because Kayleb always arrived with a project. This one was for psychology class, a survey he was administering to everyone he could corner.

"Ten questions, takes a minute," Kayleb said, dropping onto the chair across the ledger. "You owe me, after I hauled boxes all morning."

Jake took the pen. The first questions were nothing, stripes or solids, dogs or cats. Then Kayleb read one aloud while Jake followed on the page.

"Fifty dollars now, or a hundred dollars in a year?"

"Fifty now." Jake didn't even pause. "Fifty in my hand beats a promise."

"Interesting." Kayleb wrote it down with a small smile that Jake didn't like.

"What."

"Next question. A hundred dollars in six years, or fifty dollars in five?"

"A hundred in six." Jake said it just as fast, then heard himself say it and looked up. Kayleb was grinning outright now, and Ulysse had turned from the boxes he was supposed to be taping shut.

"You realize those are the same question," Ulysse said. "One year apart, both times. You just answered it two different ways."

"They are not the same question."

"They're exactly the same distance apart. One year."

"That's pernicious," Kayleb said, delighted, "how you flipped."

"It's a real thing," Ulysse said. "Present bias." He went back to his boxes.

Kayleb kept writing. "Don't impugn my survey, either, before you say the sample's rigged."

Jake pushed the clipboard away and stood up. His face felt warm, the way it did when a teacher caught him on something he hadn't studied. He went to the counter to make himself useful with the dishes that didn't need washing.

The ledger was still open when he came back to the table, and he read it to have somewhere to put his eyes. Most of it was accounts, bushels and dollars, but one page near the middle was different. His grandfather had written a note to himself in the summer he turned eighteen: Sold the river field to Nielsen for less than Vargas offered, because Vargas would pay in the spring and Nielsen paid that day. In the margin, added later in the same ink but a shakier hand, decades on: the most expensive impatience of my life. And beneath it, underlined twice, an injunction in block letters: WAIT.

Jake sat down. He read it again, then once more, and the kitchen got very quiet except for Ulysse pulling tape off the roll.

"What's the field worth now?" he asked.

Ulysse came over and looked. "The one past the culvert? With the new houses on it?" He didn't finish the math out loud, which was its own answer.

Kayleb leaned in, squinting. "That's rough." For once he wasn't grinning.

Jake turned the pages forward. Two years after the river field, there was another entry: turned down Harmon's offer, waited for the county contract, and the numbers afterward ran in a different direction entirely. His grandfather had learned it once, the way people learn things, by paying for them.

He got his phone out and called Mr. González, who had been the neighbour for forty years and had already offered, twice, to buy the corner lot where the garage stood. The first offer had been for cash at closing, quick and clean. The second, which Mr. González had mentioned almost apologetically at the funeral, was a smaller amount now and a larger one at the anniversary, when his pension came through.

"It's the July number I'll honor," Mr. González said on the phone. "You know that. And you know the cash one closes faster, if the family needs it."

"The family's not deciding this. I'm deciding my part. I want to talk about the July number."

There was a pause long enough that Jake could hear the other man breathing, could hear his own heart going.

"Come by," Mr. González said. "I'll put coffee on."

Jake hung up and looked at the ledger, at the underlined word, and at the survey still lying on the table with his two answers beside each other, $50 now and $100 in six years, the same year spent in opposite directions. He closed the clipboard, then went to the hooks by the door and took down his grandfather's jacket, the one with the good pockets.

"Tell my mom where I went," he said to Ulysse, and pulled the screen door shut behind him, holding it this time until the latch caught.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Sociologist Mark Granovetter's 1973 paper 'The Strength of Weak Ties' found that people often learned of new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends.
story:
The new classroom smelled of floor wax and cold radiators, and Laurence took the only empty desk, third row, beside a window beaded with rain. Behind her, two boys argued in low voices about whether a coffee shop downtown was hiring; the one with the green binder, Konnor, said he had asked twice and been ignored twice, and the other, Jaiveer, said that was because Konnor wore his interview shirt to gym class. Laurence kept her eyes on the board, where Ms. Fortin was writing a date, 1973, and underlining it twice.

"You've moved here from a town smaller than this one," Ms. Fortin said, not a question, pausing at Laurence's desk with the attendance sheet. "We'll sequester you in the back lab Thursday, makeup placement test, unless you'd rather do it now and get it over with." Laurence said now, please, and Ms. Fortin nodded as though that settled something between them. Their eyes met a half second longer than necessary. Laurence was almost sure they had met before, at the hardware store, a woman reaching cans of paint from a high shelf for her while her mother paid. Twice, maybe. The second time at the bus stop, an umbrella offered, a name exchanged and immediately lost.

Ms. Fortin handed back a stack of photocopied pages, warm from the machine, and one slid to Laurence's floor. She picked it up and found she had kept it. The top line read, "Mark Granovetter, 'The Strength of Weak Ties,' 1973." Below that, a single underlined sentence: people often learned of new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends.

"That's my dad's favorite paper," Jaiveer said over her shoulder at lunch, which they had invited her to without ceremony, sliding a tray to make room. "He's a sociologist. He says your close friends know everything you know. Acquaintances are the ones who know somebody you don't."

"So strangers are better than friends now," Konnor said. "Great. I'll tell my mother she raised me wrong."

"You'll tell her you should have let me beRaised by the neighbors," Jaiveer said, and both of them laughed, and Laurence laughed too, the first time in three weeks, the sound strange in her mouth like a word from her old town.

The trouble was the job itself. Her mother wanted her working by October, tuition for the community college branch, bus fare, the small arithmetic of a household that had moved for cheaper rent. Konnor had already applied at the bakery on Delancey, twice, in his good shirt, and had been told both times that the position was filled even as the HELP WANTED sign stayed up in the window. Laurence understood the shape of the thing before she could say it: if she used the woman from the bus stop, if the woman knew the bakery's owner, if a word in an aisle put Laurence ahead of Konnor, then she would have taken something from a person who had shared his lunch table with her. She turned Granovetter's sentence over all evening, annoyed at how easily it excused her. It wasn't a law of nature. It was a description of how people blunder into luck, and she could choose whether to blunder.

She did choose. On Saturday she walked to the hardware store on the chance the woman would be there, and she was, restocking shelf paper, and Laurence asked, ears hot, whether she knew anyone at the bakery on Delancey. The woman straightened, pleased. "Elaine? I've known her thirty years. Come Monday I'll call her." She wiped her hands and offered one, and her grip was dry and strong and smelled faintly of linseed oil. "I never got your name at the bus stop."

"Laurence," Laurence said. "And I have a friend who applied there first."

The woman considered this, head tilted, rain ticking on the roof above the fluorescent hum. "Then tell Elaine that too," she said. "A person who says that is worth hiring more than one who doesn't."

Monday morning, before the bell, Laurence set the photocopied page on Ms. Fortin's desk, gone soft at the edges from her coat pocket. "I think you're the woman from the bus stop," she said. "You gave me your umbrella."

"I did," Ms. Fortin said. "And I made a phone call this morning before any of you were awake. Elaine wants two people Saturday, one at the register and one doing early bake. Tell Konnor his shirt will finally be seen by the correct audience." She slid the page back across the desk. "And keep that. It reads better the second time."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Early Decision in US college admissions is binding: a student admitted with acceptable financial aid must enroll and withdraw all other applications.
story:
The letter sat in Samuel's inbox like a held breath, and he could not make himself open it in his bedroom, so he printed it and brought it to school folded into his chemistry notebook.

Mr. Hussain's room was empty during lunch except for Veer, who had claimed the desk by the radiator and was drawing veined leaves in the margin of his calculus homework, and Zaina, who was eating rice from a container and reading a brochure for a university in Massachusetts. Samuel set the folded pages on the lab bench in front of him and looked at them the way you look at a dog you suspect of biting.

"Is that it?" Veer asked, without looking up.

"That's it." The paper had arrived as an email at 5:03 in the morning. He had woken at 5:14 and known, in some vestigial part of his brain left over from an era of telegrams, that news had come in the night.

"Then open it," Zaina said. "Or don't, but stop hovering. You're making the room nervous."

He opened it. The first line contained the word congratulations, and he heard Veer say something and Zaina say something louder, and then the second paragraph began, and he read it twice, and the celebration went on around him without him in it.

"Read the rest out loud," Zaina said, and he did, and the room went quiet.

The letter offered him admission under Early Decision, which meant, the letter said plainly, that he was bound to enroll, that he had to withdraw every other application by the deadline printed below, provided the financial aid offer met a standard the letter called reasonable. His aid package was outlined on the second page. Samuel read the number there and then turned the paper over as if the reverse side might contain a correction.

"That's it?" Zaina said again, meaning something different now.

"I don't know," Samuel said. "I don't know what it means."

Zaina set down her fork. She was applying regular decision to nine schools, and she had explained her strategy to him in October with a diagram on a napkin: apply everywhere, compare every offer, choose in April like a person shopping rather than a person gambling. "You can't compare," she said slowly. "That's the whole thing. If you say yes, you withdraw everything. You never see what the other schools would have given you. You only see this."

"Then you say no," Veer said. "You say no, and you apply everywhere in the spring, like Zaina."

But Samuel was already shaking his head, because there was a third paragraph, and the third paragraph was the one he could not get past. His father had been laid off in November, and the aid office had been told, and the number on page two was not a small number. His mother had looked at their savings the way you look at a tide going out. Whatever this was, it was not an insult. It might even be generous. He simply had no way of knowing, because knowing required other letters, and other letters were exactly what he was not permitted to wait for.

"My grandfather," Samuel said, mostly to the bench, "used to talk about his patrimony. Fourteen acres he never saw, in a country he left when he was six. He used to say a man should know what he's inheriting before he signs." He laughed a little. "He was talking about land. But it's the same shape, isn't it. They're asking me to accept an inheritance I haven't counted."

Mr. Hussain came in then, collecting a mug he'd forgotten, and saw the papers. "Ah," he said, and put the mug down, and did not pick it up again. He pulled a stool over but did not sit on it. "I won't tell you what to do, Samuel. I made a decision like this once, badly, and I've never been sure whether it was badly in the way I think it was." He straightened a beaker that was already straight. "But I'll say one thing. Ask the aid office what you want to ask. Questions are free. Silence is what costs."

So Samuel spent the last twenty minutes of lunch in the hallway outside the main office, phone to his ear, listening to hold music transfigure itself from strings into something electronic and back. Zaina stood beside him with her arms folded, guarding him from the noise of the corridor as though concentration were a small animal that could be startled. Veer leaned against the trophy case, upside down reading the plaques.

When the financial aid officer finally spoke, Samuel asked his question in one long unbroken sentence, and the answer took ninety seconds, and he wrote down only four words. He read them to Zaina and Veer: appeal possible, deadline Friday.

"Then that's what you do," Zaina said.

"It's not," Samuel said. "The appeal might come back higher, and higher might still not be enough, and if I sign before I hear, I'm bound either way. And if I wait past Friday to hear first, I lose the spot." He folded the letter along its original creases. "I keep thinking there's a right answer and I just haven't found it. But maybe the right answer is just whichever one I can pay for."

"There's a wrong answer," Veer said. "There's definitely a wrong answer. Staying in this hallway forever is the wrong answer."

The bell rang. Zaina took the brochure out of her back pocket, smoothed it against her knee, and handed it to him. "Look at page nine," she said. "Housing costs. Nobody counts housing costs."

He slid the folded letter into his chemistry notebook, between stoichiometry and equilibrium, and followed her down the hall.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: The ancient Greek historian Thucydides admitted that the speeches in his history of the Peloponnesian War were not word-for-word records, but what he judged each speaker would have needed to say.
story:
Hailey had forty minutes before the library closed and a paper due at midnight, and she was still missing a quotation she'd promised her outline it would have. She spread her books across the table by the window while Everleigh guarded the seat across from her and Madisyn whispered into her phone about printing costs at the front desk, where Mr. Li was already watching them with the querulous patience of a man who had closed this building a thousand times and expected no surprises from anyone in it.

"The funeral oration," Hailey said, flipping pages. "Pericles. That famous part about how the whole city is a school for Greece. I had it highlighted, I swear, and then I wrote my whole paragraph around it."

"Then find it again," Everleigh said. "Your paragraph says the speech shows how Athenians saw themselves. You just need the words."

But the words were not behaving. In her notes she had one version, and in the big blue Loeb volume she pulled from the stacks, with Mr. Li's help and his mild remark that the return cart was not a shelf, the sentences ran differently, longer, the rhythm changed, as if someone had translated the same morning two separate ways.

"Maybe your notes came from a website," Madisyn said, coming back. "Websites don't cite. Mr. Li, is there a rule that websites have to cite?"

"There is a rule that you have to," Mr. Li said, and moved on with his cart.

Hailey read the introduction to the volume, half to procrastinate and half because the paragraph kept snagging on a phrase she didn't understand. Then she stopped skimming and actually read it. Thucydides, the historian, had admitted in his own preface that the speeches in his history of the Peloponnesian War were not word-for-word records. He had not stood in the assembly with a stenographer's ear. He had written what he judged each speaker would have needed to say.

"You look sick," Everleigh said.

"I've been quoting a ghost." Hailey turned the book so Everleigh could see the page. "This speech I built my whole argument on. Pericles probably gave some version of it, but this version, the beautiful one, is partly the historian's own construction. He says so. Right there."

"Then your paper's dead?"

Hailey wanted to say yes. It would have been a relief, almost, to be disabused of the whole project and start over with something safer, the fall of an empire, a battle, anything with dates that didn't argue back. But she had twenty minutes now, and the closing announcement would come, and her outline was on the screen with its confident little claim that the oration showed how Athenians saw themselves.

She looked at that claim again. It still felt true. The strange part was that it might be truer now, not that Athens saw itself that way, but that Thucydides judged that this was what Athens needed to hear and to believe about itself, in the first winter of a war that would run for nearly three decades. The speech was a window either way. She just had to be honest about which kind of glass.

"Madisyn, in your philosophy thing last term, didn't you argue something about how every source has a viewpoint?"

"Every source has a speaker," Madisyn said, "and every speaker wants something. I got a B-plus."

"I'll take it." Hailey opened a new paragraph and began to type, fast, her own volition and the deadline pushing in the same direction at last. She kept the quotation. She cut the sentence that called it a record. In its place she wrote that the historian himself admitted the speeches were reconstructions, and that this made the oration evidence of two minds at once, the statesman's and the historian's, each with his own judgment about what Athens was.

"Ten minutes," Mr. Li called from the front desk, not unkindly.

Everleigh read over her shoulder. "So you're saying you can't know exactly what he said."

"I'm saying I can know two things that are almost as good. What he probably said, and what a careful man writing it down thought it had to mean." Hailey reread her last sentence, found one clause she didn't believe anymore, and deleted it. The paragraph ended without a conclusion. It ended with the fact, resting there, unresolved and kind of shining.

"Email it to yourself before the wifi dies," Madisyn said. "It dies when he shuts the desk light off."

Hailey hit send. The little confirmation chime sounded through the reading room, too loud, and Mr. Li looked up from his keys.

"Sorry," she said, and closed the blue volume, and carried it back to the return cart herself.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: A table read is a seated read-through of a script by the cast, used to hear how the dialogue sounds before any staging begins.
story:
The auditorium smelled of dust and radiator paint, and the folded seats were stacked in the aisles for the spring play's set construction, so Mr. Lindqvist had them drag two long tables onto the stage itself. He announced that the final project for Drama II would be a ten-minute play drawn from a moment in each student's own life, staged at the end of May. Aaron sat near the back of the group with his notebook open and nothing written in it.

The moment he kept circling was the night his father drove four hours in a snowstorm to pick him up from a debate tournament the bus had abandoned, and the two of them had not spoken a word until a diner outside Binghamton, where his father ordered pie for both of them and then admitted he'd been laid off that afternoon. He had never told anyone about the layoff part, not even his mother, who had found out a week later from a letter. He wrote three pages that night, and the pages were terrible, and he knew they were terrible in a way he couldn't name.

Antonio found him at lunch the next day, reading the script with his thumb pressed against his temple. "You're grinding your teeth again," Antonio said. "What's wrong with it?"

"I don't know. It sounds like a play. My dad doesn't talk like a play. He said maybe nine words that whole night, and in this thing he has a speech."

"Then cut the speech."

"If I cut the speech, there's no play. There's two guys eating pie in silence for ten minutes."

Antonio pulled the notebook toward himself. "Do the thing Lindqvist keeps saying. Hear it out loud. Get people to sit and read it."

Aaron had half-listened when Mr. Lindqvist described it on the first day, something about a read-through before any staging, cast seated around a table, scripts in hand. Antonio used the term anyway, casually, as if it were nothing: "We do a table read. Sit down, read the parts, and you'll hear where it's fake." That evening, Aaron texted Massimo, who was in the class but took nothing seriously, and Massimo agreed to read the father on the condition that he could do a voice. Aaron said no voice. Massimo said a small voice.

They met on the stage after school on Thursday, when the auditorium was empty except for a janitor buffing the lobby floor. Antonio read the stage directions. Massimo read the father. Aaron read himself, which felt strange, like reciting a dream to people who hadn't had it. The early pages went fine, faster than he expected, and then they hit the diner scene, and Massimo delivered the line "A man learns what he's made of when the road turns to ice" in his small voice, and Aaron heard it, really heard it, and put his face in his hands.

"That's awful," he said. "Nobody says that."

"I said it beautifully," Massimo said.

"It's not you, it's the line. My dad said, quote, get the cherry, it's the big slice. That's it. That's the whole speech."

Antonio leaned back in the chair, balancing it on two legs the way Mr. Lindqvist always yelled at him for. "So write that."

"Then the audience doesn't know he lost his job. The line carries the information."

"Does it, though? Or does the silence carry it? Because right now the line kills it." Antonio let the chair drop forward. "You're trying to make the moment mean something out loud. But you've been going around all semester telling us subtext is the thing you valorize, and then your own dad has to announce his feelings in iambic pentameter."

Aaron laughed, then stopped laughing, because Antonio was right in a way that stung. He had spent the semester learning to read other people's scripts for what was underneath, and the one script where he actually knew what was underneath, he had flattened it. He took out a pencil and crossed out the speech, all of it, and in the margin wrote the cherry line. Underneath he wrote: he says nothing else. Let the mother's letter come later.

He got home late and found the actual letter, the real one from the company, still folded in his father's desk drawer where he'd discovered it in March and never mentioned. He didn't take it. He sat at his own desk instead and wrote his mother a note, because the play had made him honest in a way that direct conversation hadn't: "I knew before you did. I'm sorry I pretended I didn't. Ask me anything." He left it under her coffee mug for the morning, and his stomach hurt the way it had in the diner, but differently.

The next week they did a second read at the same table on the stage, and Massimo, without being asked, dropped the small voice entirely. He said get the cherry, it's the big slice, and then he was quiet for most of the rest of the scene, turning his empty coffee cup in slow circles, and the silence did what the speech had been pretending to do. Mr. Lindqvist, who had drifted in from the wings without anyone noticing, said nothing until the read ended. Then he asked Aaron whether the ending, the son telling the father about the note he'd written, was true. Aaron said some of it. He didn't say which parts, and Mr. Lindqvist nodded and wrote something in his binder.

At home his mother had left his note on the counter with one word added at the bottom in her small, careful hand: tomorrow. On Friday, Antonio found him in the auditorium rows during study hall. "Lindqvist wants us staging it in two weeks. He says the table read's done its job." Aaron looked down at the stage from the dark of the seats, the two long tables still standing under the work lights, scripts splayed open on them where they'd been left. "Then I need a cherry pie," he said.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: Adding lanes to a congested highway often fails to reduce traffic for long, because faster trips attract more driving until the new space fills; this effect is called induced demand.
story:
The flyer appeared on the corkboard outside the cafeteria on a Tuesday, three weeks before the council vote: WIDEN ROUTE 9, it said, in letters sized for people driving past at speed. Abigail read it twice, copied the meeting date into her phone, and went to fifth period, where Mr. Lavoie was collecting the rough drafts of the economics projects he had assigned before anyone cared about Route 9.

Her draft was about bus routes, or it had been until her father started coming home late. He drove delivery vans out past the county line, and lately the commute had stretched from forty minutes to well over an hour, both ways, every day. He did not complain. He ate, watched half a game, slept, and left again at five. When she asked him directly whether the new lanes would help, he said, "Can't hurt," and that answer bothered her more than a complaint would have, because he had decided not to think about it.

Terrance had decided the opposite. His mother worked two jobs and his brother had just been laid off from the hardware store, and a distribution center was rumored for the east side of town, contingent, the rumor went, on the road being widened first. "Four hundred jobs," Terrance said at lunch, tapping the flyer. "You want me to argue against four hundred jobs so your dad saves ten minutes?" He wasn't being cruel; he was being accurate, which was sometimes worse.

That night she found a message in her school inbox from Mr. Lavoie, sent to the whole class. "Several of you have chosen the Route 9 proposal," it read. "A word of caution: the intuitive answer and the evidence are not always the same thing. If you argue that more lanes must mean less traffic, be prepared to defend that claim, because the literature does not. You might begin with what happened in other cities that tried it. And a broader caution, since you are all about to be handed a vote: a project can aggrandize the people who propose it, employ the people who build it, and still fail the people who drive it. Consider who benefits and on what timeline." She read it three times, then opened her laptop and started with the search terms he had implied: widened highways, traffic after, studies.

What she found was strange at first and then obvious in the way things become obvious. Cities added lanes to congested highways, travel got faster for a while, and then the faster trips attracted more driving until the new space filled again. She sat with that for a long time, eating cold rice out of the container, watching her father's headlights come up the street an hour after dark. There was a name for it, one of the articles said, a man quoted at a transit meeting used it, and when she looked it up she wrote it on a sticky note and put it above her desk: induced demand. It sounded like something you could say out loud at a podium.

At the council meeting the following Thursday, the gymnasium smelled like floor wax and folding chairs. A man in a suit from the county transportation office showed slides of the proposed cross-section, three lanes becoming five, and talked about flow. Residents lined up at the microphone. A woman from the west side said her street already carried the overflow. The hardware store owner, Terrance's mother's old boss, said the road was choking local business. Then Terrance stood up, holding his written statement in a hand that shook only slightly, and said the east side had been promised jobs for twelve years and this was the first real offer, and he did not intend to let a room full of commuters take it away to save themselves ten minutes. Applause from one section, silence from another. He sat down without looking at Abigail.

She had not signed up to speak. She did it anyway, printing her name at the bottom of the sheet while the clerk was setting up the next presenter. At the microphone she said her father drove Route 9 twice a day and she wanted the traffic gone as much as anyone in the room. She said the evidence showed the wider road would likely fill up again within a few years, because faster trips attracted more driving until the new capacity was used up, and that this was called induced demand. She said that if the council wanted jobs, they should tie the money directly to the distribution center, transit, or anything else, rather than to lanes that would not stay empty. She said she might be wrong about the jobs part, that she had not figured out how to count them, and she would rather say so than pretend. Then she thanked them and sat down, and her ears were ringing, and a woman two rows back turned around and gave her a long look that Abigail could not interpret.

The vote was tabled for a month, pending a traffic study the county had somehow not done. In the parking lot afterward Terrance was leaning on a chain-link fence, still holding his folded statement. "You didn't say no," he said. "You said no to the lanes, not to the jobs." He looked at the paper, then at her. "Help me figure out the jobs part. You're better with the numbers." The sodium light over the gymnasium door buzzed and steadied, and Abigail pulled her jacket closed against the cold and said, "Tuesday. Bring everything you've got."
